She wanted to learn ASL to help her brother. Then she trained Girl Scouts to help others

by Marissa Greene August 23, 2026 4:00 pmAugust 21, 2026 4:33 pm

Mansfield Girl Scout Hannah Blank raised her right hand, closed in a fist, then pointed her pinky finger to the sky. 

Across the cafeteria table from her was a group of Girl Scout Juniors in teal vests who watched and waited for Blank’s next move. 

She then swooped her pinky finger down and curved up, making the shape of the letter ‘J’ in American Sign Language. 

The lesson was part of Blank’s project of almost two years teaching scouts American Sign Language. During that time, she has taught 134 scouts from Tarrant County and around the country the basics of ASL, including the alphabet, common signs, and key Girl Scout phrases. 

Blank’s efforts to teach Girl Scouts in Tarrant County and beyond sign language earned her recognition in 52 Faces of Community, the Fort Worth Report’s weekly series highlighting unsung heroes.

“If we’re in the community, we need to communicate with everybody, and there shouldn’t be a reason why a Girl Scout has to turn down helping or selling cookies to somebody because they can’t communicate with them,” Blank said. 

Blank’s interest in learning sign language grew from her desire to better communicate with her younger brother, who has Down syndrome and is hard of hearing, she said. 

She developed a passion for sign language during her freshman year of high school and joined the ASL club, which was led by a deaf teacher. 

“Talking to her and getting to know her experiences really made me want to do something to help,” Blank said. 

Blank taught Brownies, Juniors and scouts at other levels the basics: their ABCs and how to sign common phrases like “How are you?” and “What’s your name?” She also taught the Girl Scout Promise in sign language. 

Her project included in-person lessons at Girl Scout events like Badge Fest and virtual meetings with a North Carolina troop. Blank’s project also included a Girl Scout night at Tarrant County College to bring an event called Deaf Deaf World, an immersive, no-talking simulation where participants navigate daily tasks using only sign language. 

“I’ve always loved doing community service or volunteering for something, so it felt right to try to do it,” Blank said.

Blank was one of 16 scouts in her Girl Scout council who recently received the Gold Award in 2025 for her efforts. The award is open to high school girls in grades 9 through 12 who are registered as a Girl Scout Senior or Ambassador and wants to address a need or issue in their community, according to their website. 

The Gold Award is the highest highest honor a Girl Scout can earn, said Maria Gregorio, marketing and public relations coordinator for Girl Scouts of Texas Oklahoma Plains.

The project addressed a national and global need, particularly among deaf Girl Scouts in Puerto Rico and Qatar, Gregorio wrote in her nomination. She said she nominated Blank because her initiative helped peers build confidence and empathy toward those with differing communication needs.

Gregorio believes Blank’s project will be remembered for its far-reaching impact, especially among younger scouts. “I think that will be the much more lasting legacy of what she’s done,” she said.

Blank, 19, is studying forensic science at Texas A&M University. While she is no longer on cookie-selling detail, she said she will always be a scout volunteer and big sister. 

“As a Girl Scout, I’m able to connect with more people who are also in the organization,” Blank said. “As a sister, it gives me a better way to communicate with my brother.” 

Marissa Greene is the faith and fellowships editor at the Fort Worth Report. You can contact her at marissa.greene@fortworthreport.org.
